title: Reading a line and validating it
goal: Read one integer safely from a line and explain why the whole record is suitable for calculation.

prerequisites.text: Recall why M1 checks data before division.

terms.title: Record
terms.definition: The bytes before a newline. A final non-empty record may end at end of input.

terms.title: End of file (EOF)
terms.definition: A distinct value returned by getchar when input runs out or reading fails. ferror distinguishes these cases.

terms.title: Unparsed tail
terms.definition: Characters after the number. This program permits only whitespace there.

terms.title: Range
terms.definition: The values the task accepts. Check it before conversion to int.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: A charging rack accepts between 1 and 48 cells. An operator enters a line and might accidentally append a unit or press Enter without supplying data. Separate reading a record, recognising a number and checking the rule for the rack.
A 64-byte buffer holds 63 text bytes and a terminating null byte. The newline is consumed but not stored. A line that exceeds capacity is rejected as a whole, even if its prefix would be valid.
READ_OK, READ_END and READ_BAD mean “value ready”, “no new record” and “record rejected”. The library uses end as a bookmark in the string. The later pointers module explains its representation.

The read_line and read_integer functions are provided. Follow the result from the line to the number and its remainder, then to the range check and status. In main, decide what to print for each status.

Each validation answers a separate question. `end == line` detects missing digits, the range checks the value, and the tail check detects extra text. A range check alone gives no information about the tail.

sections.title: A valid cell count
paragraphs: The input contains a space and a tab before 18 and a space after it. Trace this input in the listing and predict what will be stored in cells.
read_line limits and records bytes. strtol reads a decimal integer and marks the position after the digits. Only after all checks does read_integer store the integer and return READ_OK.
steps: Read bytes up to a newline or EOF. ferror distinguishes a stream error from normal end of input.
Reset errno before strtol. If there are no digits, end stays at the start. An oversized number can cause ERANGE.
After the range check, skip trailing whitespace. Any remaining character is extra data.
main reads cells only if read_integer returned READ_OK.

sections.title: The number parses but the record fails
paragraphs: For 18A, strtol returns 18 and the bookmark points to A. Checking only the number would accept an incorrect record.
Do not store the result of getchar in char. EOF could become indistinguishable from a data byte. Compare it with an int result.
strtol expects the address of the variable end. Passing end instead of &end causes an incompatible type diagnostic. The rejected fragment is for reading compiler output.

sections.title: Separate numeric syntax from the input contract
paragraphs: Trace the listing again with 0 in place of 18. The numeric syntax still parses, but the rack rule rejects zero.
A blank record differs from an empty stream. Both produce invalid here, but in an empty stream the program has not read a record.

selfcheck.feedback: A final non-empty record can be used as the number 18. With no data, the helper reports READ_END.

practice.title: An operator-entered thermometer reading
practice.task: Complete the tail check in the supplied helper. The program reads the first line with one integer from −40 to 60, allowing surrounding whitespace. Print temperature followed by the valid value. Print invalid for a rejected record.
practice.hint: After the isspace loop, end points to the terminating null or the first extra character.
criteria: Reject the tail in 12C and a second number on the same line.
Do not print data from a rejected record. Accept surrounding whitespace.
CRLF and the null byte are checked with exact input fixtures. The browser input box cannot reproduce these cases reliably.

steps.expected: The starter incorrectly accepts its numeric prefix.

steps.action: Check the character after trailing whitespace.

steps.why: Check both boundaries and one value outside them.

exercises.title: Transfer a boundary check
exercises.task: Give a line containing -1 that is rejected because of its tail, then a line with the same number that is accepted. Explain the difference.
criteria: The explanation distinguishes the value from the record.

teaching.scene: An operator enters the number of charging cells on one line. The result should make clear whether the program accepted the entire record, including any spaces after the number.

predict.prompt: The sample has a space and tab before 18 and a space after it. What does strtol consume, and what prints after the tail check?
predict.answer: strtol skips the leading whitespace and reads 18. end points at the trailing space. The loop skips it and reaches '\0'. The value is in 1…48 and the output is cells 18.

apply.prompt: An operator enters `18 cells`. How can you verify that the number was recognized and the record was still rejected?
apply.answer: strtol returns 18, then skipping the space leaves end at c. Non-whitespace remains before '\0', so expect invalid.

practice.strategy: Separate reading the record, parsing the number and checking the tail. Trace where end stops after skipping whitespace. Test both ends of the range and a number followed by a unit.
practice.diagnosis: If `12C` gives temperature 12, the numeric prefix already parsed. Inspect the byte at end after skipping whitespace. A complete record reaches '\0'.

syntax.explanation: strtol sets end to the first unparsed byte. After whitespace is skipped, the byte at that address reveals whether part of the record remains.
syntax.mistake: An allowed numeric value establishes only the number. In `18 units`, the remaining text contains letters.
